ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The inclusion criteria were: (1) studies published between 1990 and 2023; (2) experimental tasks focusing on phonological, semantic, or language-control processing; (3) experimental materials restricted to lexical stimuli; (4) participants were healthy bilinguals without reading disorders.

After reviewing the brain-imaging results, further exclusion criteria were applied: (1) participants were bimodal bilinguals; (2) activation coordinates were incompletely reported (e.g., region-of-interest analyses) or not reported at all; (3) contrast conditions did not match our research interests.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> The inclusion criteria were: (1) studies published between 1990 and 2023; (2) experimental tasks focusing on phonological, semantic, or language-control processing; (3) experimental materials restricted to lexical stimuli; (4) participants were healthy bilinguals without reading disorders.

> After reviewing the brain-imaging results, further exclusion criteria were applied: (1) participants were bimodal bilinguals; (2) activation coordinates were incompletely reported (e.g., region-of-interest analyses) or not reported at all; (3) contrast conditions did not match our research interests.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Whether bilinguals share the same neural mechanisms for processing their first language (L1) and second language (L2) is a question of broad interest to researchers.
Existing studies have accumulated substantial evidence, yet findings remain divergent.
The primary sources of inconsistency lie in the language distance between bilinguals' L1 and L2, as well as differences in experimental tasks.

Leveraging the advantages of meta-analysis, the present study examined brain activation patterns during L1 and L2 lexical processing in two groups of bilinguals: Chinese-English bilinguals with distant language distance (logographically-alphabetic) and alphabeticalphabetic bilinguals with close language distance-across different tasks (phonological and semantic).

Results showed that in phonological tasks, Chinese-English bilinguals recruited the left inferior parietal lobule/supramarginal gyrus more for L2, a region implicated in orthography-tophonology conversion; in contrast, alphabetic bilinguals with close language distance shared overlapping neural mechanisms for L1 and L2.
In semantic tasks, Chinese-English bilinguals engaged the left middle frontal gyrus and left precuneus more for L1 to support orthography-tosemantics conversion.

In contrast, alphabetic bilinguals recruited the left middle temporal gyrus more for L1 for phonology-to-semantics conversion, and engaged language-control regions including the left middle frontal gyrus/inferior frontal gyrus, insula, and inferior parietal lobule more for L2.

Further comparisons of brain activation during language-switching tasks between the two bilingual groups also revealed that alphabetic bilinguals with close language distance required greater involvement of executive control regions.

Collectively, these findings indicate that the differential brain activation patterns observed when bilinguals process L1 and L2 arise from differences in underlying cognitive processes, jointly driven by language distance and task demands.
Whether the bilingual brain reads words in two languages via shared neural mechanisms is a question that has garnered extensive attention and debate among researchers.

Some investigators argue that bilinguals share the same neural network for processing their first language (L1) and second language (L2) (Brignoni-Perez et al., 2020; Hernandez et al., 2015), whereas others contend that bilinguals develop a second-language-specific neural network (Kim et al., 2016; Nichols & Joanisse, 2016).

text.text: The long-standing divergence in findings stems, on the one hand, from the fact that the language distance (i.e., linguistic similarity) between L1 and L2 modulates whether bilinguals share overlapping neural substrates (Cargnelutti et al., 2022; Dong et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2016; Li et al., 2021; Shen & Del Tufo, 2022).

text.text: On the other hand, existing results have been obtained under specific processing tasks, and bilinguals require distinct neural networks when performing phonological, semantic, and executive-control tasks (Comstock & Oliver, 2021; Sulpizio et al., 2020).

text.text: Therefore, it is necessary to examine, across different task conditions, whether bilinguals with varying language distances share a common neural network for lexical processing in both languages.
This complex issue is difficult to resolve through individual experimental studies alone; the present study leverages the advantages of meta-analysis to address it in depth.
Language distance refers to the difference in orthographic depth between two languages, reflecting the degree of similarity between them.
Differing orthographic depths between bilinguals' languages may entail distinct underlying processing mechanisms (Oliver et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Differing orthographic depths between bilinguals' languages may entail distinct underlying processing mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Oliver et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Chinese characters are morphograms (logographs) whose orthography-to-phonology correspondences are irregular; they have deep orthographic depth and are considered opaque scripts.

In contrast, alphabetic scripts such as Spanish and English are phonograms (alphabetic scripts) with relatively shallow orthographic depth; among them, Spanish can be decoded directly from orthography to phonology and is thus a transparent orthography.
Previous studies have shown that orthographic depth influences phonological and semantic access during lexical processing (Mei et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Previous studies have shown that orthographic depth influences phonological and semantic access during lexical processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Mei et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">Yang et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: For deep-orthography scripts like Chinese, phonological processing relies more on the lexical route, tending to access semantics via orthography (Han & Bi, 2009; Tan et al., 2005); for shallow-orthography scripts like Spanish and English, phonological processing relies more on the sublexical route, tending to access semantics via phonology (Braun et al., 2009; Mei et al., 2015).

However, few existing studies have distinguished task demands, leaving the underlying mechanisms of these effects unclear.

Findings indicate that task demands can modulate bilingual activation networks; bilinguals recruit distinct neural networks when performing phonological, semantic, and executive-control tasks (Comstock & Oliver, 2021; Sulpizio et al., 2020).

text.text: For example, Chinese-English bilinguals showed L1-L2 differences in bilateral inferior parietal lobule and bilateral postcentral gyrus during an orthographic task, whereas in a semantic task, differences emerged in the left middle frontal gyrus, middle temporal gyrus, and right inferior frontal gyrus (Ding et al., 2003).

text.text: The specific computational demands hypothesis posits that brain regions activated by L2 are the same as those activated by L1, and that activation differences between L2 and L1 arise solely from different computational demands (Perani & Abutalebi, 2005).

text.text: Bilingual activation differences observed under specific tasks are accordingly linked to the underlying computational requirements, which are shaped by both bottom-up linguistic properties and top-down task demands (Dang et al., 2024).

text.text: Therefore, it is necessary to examine in detail the mechanisms by which language distance influences bilingual processing in conjunction with task demands.

Some researchers have attempted to explore the effect of language distance on the neural mechanisms of lexical processing under phonological tasks, and have found that the closer the language distance between L1 and L2, the smaller the activation differences between the two languages.

For instance, when Korean-Chinese-English trilinguals performed a visual lexical rhyming judgment task, Korean and English (with close language distance) showed differential activation only in the left inferior frontal gyrus, whereas Korean and Chinese (with distant language distance) engaged differential activation across multiple regions including frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes, leading the authors to conclude that language distance modulates bilingual activation differences in phonological processing (Kim et al., 2016).
text.formatted: For instance, when Korean-Chinese-English trilinguals performed a visual lexical rhyming judgment task, Korean and English (with close language distance) showed differential activation only in the left inferior frontal gyrus, whereas Korean and Chinese (with distant language distance) engaged differential activation across multiple regions including frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes, leading the authors to conclude that language distance modulates bilingual activation differences in phonological processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Kim et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Languages with small language distance tend to recruit similar phonological processing pathways, and the activated phonological regions are consequently more similar.

This interpretation is supported by representational similarity analysis: in a visual word naming task with Uyghur-Chinese-English trilinguals, representational similarity in phonological regions between Uyghur and English (close distance) was significantly greater than that between Uyghur and Chinese (distant distance) (Dong et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This interpretation is supported by representational similarity analysis: in a visual word naming task with Uyghur-Chinese-English trilinguals, representational similarity in phonological regions between Uyghur and English (close distance) was significantly greater than that between Uyghur and Chinese (distant distance) <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Dong et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These studies suggest that under phonological tasks, bilinguals with close language distance employ similar phonological processing pathways and show greater neural overlap.
To date, no study has systematically investigated the impact of language distance on brain activation patterns in bilinguals under semantic tasks.

Existing evidence has shown that under semantic task demands, L1 activates more semantic-processing regions, whereas L2 recruits more executive-control regions (Comstock & Oliver, 2021; Sulpizio et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Existing evidence has shown that under semantic task demands, L1 activates more semantic-processing regions, whereas L2 recruits more executive-control regions <ref type="bibr">(Comstock & Oliver, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Sulpizio et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This difference may be related to the orthographic depth and language distance between bilinguals' L1 and L2.

According to the orthographic depth hypothesis, shallow-orthography scripts (e.g., English, Spanish) have regular orthography-to-phonology correspondences, leading readers to access semantics preferentially via phonological mediation (Braun et al., 2009; Tan & Perfetti, 1999); in contrast, deep-orthography scripts like Chinese have more direct orthography-to-semantics mappings, so readers may rely primarily on orthographic information for semantic access (Han & Bi, 2009; Law et al., 2006).
text.formatted: According to the orthographic depth hypothesis, shallow-orthography scripts (e.g., English, Spanish) have regular orthography-to-phonology correspondences, leading readers to access semantics preferentially via phonological mediation <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Braun et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Tan & Perfetti, 1999)</ref>; in contrast, deep-orthography scripts like Chinese have more direct orthography-to-semantics mappings, so readers may rely primarily on orthographic information for semantic access <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Han & Bi, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Law et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, the language distance between bilinguals' languages may influence the semantic neural pathways engaged during semantic processing, making language distance a potential key factor modulating L1-L2 activation differences in bilinguals.
Language control processing is a topic of broad interest in bilingual research.
How language distance affects bilingual language control remains debated, giving rise to two opposing hypotheses.

One is the cross-language interference hypothesis (Coderre & van Heuven, 2014; Radman et al., 2021), which proposes that the smaller the language distance between L1 and L2, the stronger the cross-linguistic interference, and thus the more language-control resources are required.
text.formatted: One is the cross-language interference hypothesis <ref type="bibr">(Coderre & van Heuven, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Radman et al., 2021)</ref>, which proposes that the smaller the language distance between L1 and L2, the stronger the cross-linguistic interference, and thus the more language-control resources are required.

text.text: Researchers comparing behavioural and electrophysiological responses of bilinguals with different language distances during executive-control tasks found that bilinguals with close language distance showed shorter reaction times and larger ERP amplitudes, indicating greater executive-control engagement (Coderre & van Heuven, 2014; Radman et al., 2021).

text.text: An opposing view is the cross-language facilitation hypothesis (Costa et al., 2008; Finkbeiner et al., 2006), which argues that the smaller the language distance, the more shared linguistic representations, thereby facilitating language selection and requiring fewer language-control resources.

text.text: However, it is difficult to examine the joint effects of language distance and task demands within a single experimental design through empirical studies.

Meta-analysis, by contrast, can integrate data from multiple studies and simultaneously assess the influence of multiple variables, thereby effectively disentangling complex scientific issues involving multi-factor interactions (Eickhoff et al., 2009).

text.text: Moreover, meta-analysis performs quantitative statistical analyses on activation coordinates reported in a large number of studies, identifies consistency in spatial patterns, reduces inter-study heterogeneity, and enhances the robustness and reproducibility of conclusions (Fox et al., 1998; Wager et al., 2005).

text.text: Several previous studies have attempted to use meta-analysis to investigate the effect of language distance on bilingual processing.
For instance, Li et al. (2021) examined the modulatory role of language distance on brain activation during reading in bilinguals.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Li et al. (2021)</ref> examined the modulatory role of language distance on brain activation during reading in bilinguals.

text.text: Another meta-analysis examined the influence of language distance on activation in language-control regions (Cargnelutti et al., 2022).

text.text: However, these studies did not distinguish task demands, leaving the mechanisms underlying the effect of language distance on bilingual processing unclear.
Research has shown that task demands can modulate the neural networks engaged in bilingual processing (Sulpizio et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Research has shown that task demands can modulate the neural networks engaged in bilingual processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Sulpizio et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Recent multivariate pattern analyses have also found that task demands induce changes in bilingual neural activation patterns, indicating that task demands are a key variable that warrants attention when investigating the neural mechanisms of bilingual processing (Li et al., 2023).

text.text: Therefore, the present study employed meta-analysis to concurrently examine the effects of language distance and task demands on brain activation during lexical processing in bilinguals.

Specifically, by comparing brain activations between Chinese-English bilinguals (distant language distance) and alphabetic-alphabetic bilinguals (close language distance) across phonological, semantic, and language-switching tasks, we aimed to elucidate the underlying mechanisms by which language distance and task demands modulate bilingual processing.

Considering the processing requirements of different tasks and the differences in linguistic properties between L1 and L2, we formulated the following predictions: (1) In phonological tasks, because both L1 and L2 in alphabetic bilinguals with close language distance rely on orthography-to-phonology conversion, activation differences between the two languages in phonological regions should be relatively small, whereas Chinese-English bilinguals with distant language distance should exhibit larger activation differences.
(2) In semantic tasks, bilinguals with distant language distance engage different processing pathways for L1 and L2, and thus should show greater differences in semantic-processing regions.

(3) In language-switching tasks, by comparing activation differences between the two bilingual groups in language-control-related regions, particularly in executive-control regions such as frontal and parietal cortices, we can examine whether L1-L2 linguistic similarity exerts a facilitating or interfering effect, thereby further testing the cross-language interference hypothesis versus the cross-language facilitation hypothesis.
A literature search was conducted in databases (Web of Science, PubMed, and CNKI) using the keywords "bilingual" and "neuroimaging" to retrieve studies published before May 2023.
The retrieved records were screened through a two-step process of inclusion and exclusion.

The inclusion criteria were: (1) studies published between 1990 and 2023; (2) experimental tasks focusing on phonological, semantic, or language-control processing; (3) experimental materials restricted to lexical stimuli; (4) participants were healthy bilinguals without reading disorders.

After reviewing the brain-imaging results, further exclusion criteria were applied: (1) participants were bimodal bilinguals; (2) activation coordinates were incompletely reported (e.g., region-of-interest analyses) or not reported at all; (3) contrast conditions did not match our research interests.
Ultimately, 74 studies met the inclusion criteria.

To evaluate the methodological quality of the included studies, we established a quality assessment checklist comprising 4 dimensions and 12 items, based on the best-practice reporting standards in neuroimaging (the COBIDAS guidelines).

The dimensions covered: (1) experimental design (sample-size reporting, task control, between-group matching); (2) data processing and preprocessing (procedural transparency, spatial normalization, motion-control measures); (3) statistical analysis (multiple-comparison correction, software reporting, model adequacy); and (4) result reporting and transparency (coordinate completeness, spatial consistency, data-sharing statements).
Compliance with each item was recorded as "yes" or "no".
The results showed that the vast majority of studies (81.1%, 60/74) were of high quality (score ≥ 10), while the remaining (18.9%, 14/74) were of moderate quality (scores7~9).
These findings provide methodological support for the robustness of the conclusions drawn in this meta-analysis.
We focused primarily on the neural mechanisms underlying three types of experimental tasks in bilinguals: phonological processing, semantic processing, and language switching.

Phonological processing tasks primarily involve the extraction and analysis of lexical phonological information, including rhyming judgment, overt reading, and homophone matching tasks (Wu et al., 2012).

The present study employed a meta-analytic approach to investigate how language distance between bilinguals' L1 and L2 affects the degree of shared neural mechanisms during lexical processing under different experimental tasks.
The results showed that the closer the language distance between L2 and L1, the greater the overlap in brain activation, and that experimental tasks modulate this degree of shared activation.

Specifically, in phonological tasks, Chinese-English bilinguals (with distant language distance) exhibited greater activation in the left inferior parietal lobule/supramarginal gyrus for L2 than for L1, whereas alphabetic-script bilinguals (with close language distance) recruited the same neural network for L1 and L2.

In semantic tasks, Chinese-English bilinguals showed greater L1-related activation (relative to L2) in the left middle frontal gyrus and left precuneus; for alphabetic-script bilinguals, L1 recruited the middle portion of the left superior temporal gyrus more, while L2 recruited language-control regions including the left inferior frontal gyrus/middle frontal gyrus, insula, and inferior parietal lobule to a greater extent.
The language-switching task also revealed that alphabetic-script bilinguals required greater recruitment of executive-control regions.
These findings indicate that task demands modulate neural network engagement in a top-down manner, whereas language distance influences language processing and language control in a bottom-up manner.

Further analysis suggests that task demands and language distance jointly modulate the underlying processing demands; consequently, it is essentially these underlying processing demands that dynamically shape the neural mechanisms of bilingual lexical processing.
A detailed discussion is presented below.

In the phonological tasks, the present study found that Chinese-English bilinguals with distant language distance showed greater activation in the left inferior parietal lobule/supramarginal gyrus for L2 than for L1, whereas alphabetic-script bilinguals with close language distance activated the same neural network for both L1 and L2.

This is consistent with previous findings. Kim et al. (2016) compared brain activation between Korean and English (close language distance) and between Korean and Chinese (distant language distance) during a visual lexical rhyming judgment task, and found that activation differences were smaller for the close-distance language pair.

(2016)</ref> compared brain activation between Korean and English (close language distance) and between Korean and Chinese (distant language distance) during a visual lexical rhyming judgment task, and found that activation differences were smaller for the close-distance language pair.

text.text: Our finding that alphabetic-script bilinguals with close language distance activated overlapping neural networks for L1 and L2 further supports the notion that, in phonological tasks, the closer the language distance, the more similar the phonological processing pathways used by bilinguals, and thus the smaller the activation differences.

Mei and colleagues have shown that the left inferior parietal lobule/supramarginal gyrus is a key region in the dorsal phonological pathway, primarily subserving sublexical orthography-to-phonology conversion, which is critical for phonological processing of alphabetic scripts such as English (Mei et al., 2014; Mei et al., 2015).

Regarding the function of the left middle frontal gyrus, studies have identified it as subserving semantic processing (Tan et al., 2000) or orthography-to-semantics mapping (Tan et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2012), while the left precuneus has been implicated in orthographic processing (Liu & Cao, 2016; Sun et al., 2015).

text.text: In the present study, the co-activation of the left precuneus and left middle frontal gyrus during L1 processing in Chinese-English bilinguals supports the view that this circuit is involved in orthography-to-semantics conversion.

Because Chinese characters are morphograms with more direct orthography-to-semantics mappings, readers rely preferentially on the orthographic route for semantic access (Han & Bi, 2009); thus, L1 processing in Chinese-English bilinguals recruits the left middle frontal gyrus (associated with orthography-to-semantics mapping) and the left precuneus (associated with orthographic processing) to a greater extent.

text.text: It is noteworthy that in semantic tasks, alphabetic-script bilinguals also showed greater L2-related activation in executive-control regions including the left inferior frontal gyrus/middle frontal gyrus, insula, and inferior parietal lobule.

text.text: The phonological tasks in this study primarily involved overt reading and rhyming judgment, which are relatively low in difficulty and require fewer executive-control resources; in contrast, semantic tasks mainly consisted of lexical decision and semantic judgment, which require participants to recruit greater executive-control resources to complete the decision-making process, thereby activating language-control regions (e.g., the frontoparietal control network) more extensively.

More importantly, the present study also revealed the influence of linguistic properties on bilingual executive control in the language-switching task, manifested as greater activation in the frontoparietal control network-including the left inferior frontal gyrus, middle frontal gyrus, and inferior parietal lobule-in alphabetic-script bilinguals with close language distance.

This finding further corroborates the observation in semantic tasks that alphabetic-script bilinguals recruited more language-control regions during L2 processing, indicating that bilinguals with close language distance require greater executive-control resources.

Previous studies comparing behavioural and electrophysiological responses of bilinguals with different language distances during executive-control tasks found that bilinguals with close language distance exhibited shorter reaction times and larger ERP amplitudes, suggesting stronger executive-control engagement (Coderre & van Heuven, 2014; Radman et al., 2021).

text.text: The present neuroimaging finding of greater frontoparietal control activation in alphabetic-script bilinguals, together with these earlier results, supports the cross-language interference hypothesis, which posits that bilinguals with closer language distance experience stronger cross-linguistic interference and thus require more executive-control resources.
In addition, the present study found that Chinese-English bilinguals showed greater activation in the left lingual gyrus and right hippocampus/caudate nucleus during language-switching tasks.

text.text: It should be noted, however, that the language-distance effects observed in this study cannot entirely rule out the potential influence of proficiency.

Although we grouped bilinguals by language distance (Cargnelutti et al., 2022; Li et al., 2021) and observed differential brain activation between the two groups, the lack of a unified proficiency assessment standard for direct comparison between groups means that the potential influence of proficiency cannot be completely excluded.

text.text: Proficiency reflects the learner's knowledge and ability to use the target language, whereas language distance refers to the degree of similarity between two languages.

Currently, there is relative consensus regarding the effect of proficiency on bilingual processing: studies have shown that, compared with highly proficient bilinguals, low-proficiency bilinguals require more attentional and selection resources (Cargnelutti et al., 2019; Grant et al., 2015; Sebastian et al., 2011).

text.text: In the present study, both semantic and language-switching tasks revealed greater activation in the left inferior frontal gyrus, middle frontal gyrus, and inferior parietal lobule in alphabetic-script bilinguals.

Previous studies have found that the left inferior and middle frontal gyri are sensitive to phonological competition (Hsieh et al., 2017; Matsuo et al., 2010), and the left inferior parietal lobule is associated with stimulus-based language conflict (van Heuven et al., 2008).

text.text: Thus, our findings may more likely reflect stronger cross-linguistic interference arising from closer language distance in alphabetic-script bilinguals, rather than increased attentional and selection resources due to lower proficiency.
Future studies should disentangle proficiency levels to further clarify the independent and interactive effects of these two variables on bilingual neural mechanisms.

The present study found that differences in brain activation between bilinguals' two languages during lexical processing are related to differences in the underlying processing demands specific to each task.

For instance, the left inferior parietal lobule/supramarginal gyrus, which is responsible for sublexical orthography-to-phonology conversion (Mei et al., 2015), is critically important for phonological processing of alphabetic scripts such as English; accordingly, Chinese-English bilinguals showed greater activation in this region when processing L2 in phonological tasks.

text.text: Similarly, the left middle frontal gyrus is associated with orthography-to-semantics mapping for Chinese characters (Wu et al., 2012) and is crucial for semantic access in Chinese; thus, Chinese-English bilinguals recruited this region more during L1 processing in semantic tasks.

text.text: These findings indicate that it is essentially the underlying processing demands that dynamically modulate the neural mechanisms of bilingual lexical processing.

At the same time, these underlying processing demands are jointly shaped by task demands and stimulus properties, as reflected in the fact that activation in reading-related regions is influenced by the interaction between task demands and stimulus attributes (Pattamadilok et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2012).

This suggests that the neural mechanisms of bilingual lexical processing are the result of dynamic adaptation to task demands and stimulus properties, jointly modulated by both factors.

In summary, the present study investigated the neural mechanisms of bilingual lexical processing from the perspective of the interaction between linguistic properties and task demands, revealing that bilingual lexical processing exhibits both cross-linguistic commonality and language-specificity.

The core of this dynamic activation lies in the interaction between task demands and linguistic properties, which together shape the underlying processing demands and give rise to dynamic activation differences between the two languages.

Recent studies employing multivariate analysis approaches (e.g., MVPA, RSA) have also found that bilinguals activate overlapping brain regions, yet show independent representational patterns at the finer voxel-wise level (Brignoni-Perez et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2017), and that these representational patterns are dynamic, modulated by linguistic properties (Dong et al., 2021; Hou et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2024), task demands (Li et al., 2023), and other factors.

text.text: The present study, at the level of brain activation, reveals that bilinguals share a common neural substrate, and that activation differences between the two languages are dynamically modulated by the underlying processing demands.
By employing a meta-analytic approach, the present study examined the effects of language distance and task demands on the neural mechanisms of bilingual lexical processing.

Our findings provide empirical support for the specific computational demands hypothesis (Perani & Abutalebi, 2005), which posits that brain regions recruited by L2 are identical to those recruited by L1, and that activation differences between L2 and L1 arise solely from differential computational demands.
text.formatted: Our findings provide empirical support for the specific computational demands hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Perani & Abutalebi, 2005)</ref>, which posits that brain regions recruited by L2 are identical to those recruited by L1, and that activation differences between L2 and L1 arise solely from differential computational demands.

text.text: Specifically, in phonological tasks, alphabetic-script bilinguals activated the same brain regions for both languages, indicating that when underlying processing demands are identical, the neural substrates for L1 and L2 are also shared.

Furthermore, Chinese-English bilinguals showed greater L2-related activation in the left supramarginal gyrus (associated with orthography-to-phonology conversion; Mei et al., 2015) during phonological tasks, and greater L1-related activation in the left middle frontal gyrus (associated with orthography-to-semantics mapping; Wu et al., 2012) during semantic tasks.
text.formatted: Furthermore, Chinese-English bilinguals showed greater L2-related activation in the left supramarginal gyrus (associated with orthography-to-phonology conversion; <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Mei et al., 2015)</ref> during phonological tasks, and greater L1-related activation in the left middle frontal gyrus (associated with orthography-to-semantics mapping; <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">Wu et al., 2012)</ref> during semantic tasks.

text.text: These findings indicate that activation differences between the two languages are tied to the specific computational demands required by each language in a given task.

Our results also provide insights into the ongoing debate between the language-universal view (Feng et al., 2020; Nakamura et al., 2012; Rueckl et al., 2015) and the language-specific view (Brennan et al., 2013; Zhan et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2014) from a bilingual perspective.
text.formatted: Our results also provide insights into the ongoing debate between the language-universal view <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Feng et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Nakamura et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Rueckl et al., 2015)</ref> and the language-specific view <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Brennan et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">Zhan et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">Zhao et al., 2014)</ref> from a bilingual perspective.

text.text: The language-universal view holds that there exists a common reading mechanism across writing systems.

In line with this view, our study found that both languages in bilinguals activated typical language-processing regions, suggesting that the neural substrates involved are shared across different languages.
The language-specific view, on the other hand, maintains that different writing systems recruit specialised reading mechanisms.
Supporting this view, our findings showed that Chinese-English bilinguals recruited specific brain regions to accommodate the unique properties of each script.

A recent study also pointed out that although there are common processing principles across all writing systems, readers of different orthographies naturally adapt to the specific properties of their script for efficient comprehension of written text (Li et al., 2022).
text.formatted: A recent study also pointed out that although there are common processing principles across all writing systems, readers of different orthographies naturally adapt to the specific properties of their script for efficient comprehension of written text <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Li et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The present study provides neural-level evidence for this perspective and enriches our understanding of language processing.
The following issues warrant further discussion and investigation:

First, although we observed an interaction between language distance and task demands, the ALE meta-analysis is essentially a method for estimating and contrasting activation under specific conditions; it cannot directly estimate the interaction effect of "language distance × task demands" within a unified statistical model as experimental studies can.
Our inference regarding the interaction was primarily derived from contrast analyses under different conditions, followed by indirect logical integration and interpretation.

Future studies could employ more refined experimental designs combined with multifactorial ANOVA to directly test this interaction empirically, thereby advancing the field toward a deeper stage of inquiry.
Second, the ALE meta-analysis provides only information at the level of regional brain activation and cannot further explore functional collaboration between brain regions.

In recent years, brain network analyses have revealed that bilingual experience may be associated with more efficient and flexible reorganization and reconfiguration of brain networks (Feng et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In recent years, brain network analyses have revealed that bilingual experience may be associated with more efficient and flexible reorganization and reconfiguration of brain networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Feng et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wu et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, although bilinguals and monolinguals activate overlapping brain regions, bilinguals show stronger functional connectivity between the left superior temporal gyrus and left lingual gyrus, as well as between the left middle frontal gyrus and left anterior cingulate cortex (Brignoni-Pérez et al., 2022).
text.formatted: For instance, although bilinguals and monolinguals activate overlapping brain regions, bilinguals show stronger functional connectivity between the left superior temporal gyrus and left lingual gyrus, as well as between the left middle frontal gyrus and left anterior cingulate cortex <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brignoni-Pérez et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Other studies have also found that bilingual experience modulates functional connectivity both within language regions (Oliver et al., 2017) and between language and executive-control regions (Gurunandan et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Other studies have also found that bilingual experience modulates functional connectivity both within language regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Oliver et al., 2017)</ref> and between language and executive-control regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Gurunandan et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Future research could take the brain regions identified in this study-those modulated by underlying processing demands-as regions of interest, and further investigate the impact of these processing demands on functional interactions across brain networks.
Third, the present study focused primarily on lexical-level processing; whether the conclusions can be generalized to sentence-and discourse-level processing remains to be verified.

Previous studies have shown that as the reading unit expands from words to more natural sentences and passages, readers place greater emphasis on semantic and syntactic integration at larger units, while phonological and semantic access for smaller units such as words becomes more automatic, thereby reducing cross-linguistic differences (Wang et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Previous studies have shown that as the reading unit expands from words to more natural sentences and passages, readers place greater emphasis on semantic and syntactic integration at larger units, while phonological and semantic access for smaller units such as words becomes more automatic, thereby reducing cross-linguistic differences <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">(Wang et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies could compare bilingual activation across different reading units to further explore the neural mechanisms of bilingual processing at a more detailed level.
Finally, bilingual executive control is a topic of broad interest among researchers (Abutalebi et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2020; Tao et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Finally, bilingual executive control is a topic of broad interest among researchers <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Abutalebi et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Liu et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Tao et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Although the present study provides preliminary evidence for the influence of language distance on bilingual executive control, the generalizability of our conclusions is limited by the relative homogeneity of the experimental paradigms included.

Future research could combine proficiency measures with diverse experimental paradigms (e.g., attentional selection, interference suppression) to conduct a more comprehensive and in-depth analysis of this issue.

In addition, language-switching tasks are relatively less correlated with language properties such as phonology and semantics; it is worth reflecting on what kind of processing demands the cross-linguistic differences observed in this task actually reflect.

The present study simultaneously focused on language distance and task demands, and employed a meta-analytic approach to systematically examine brain activation in Chinese-English bilinguals and alphabetic-script bilinguals during phonological, semantic, and language-switching tasks.

By comparing bilingual activation patterns between the two groups under different task demands, we found that the closer the language distance, the smaller the activation differences between L1 and L2 in language-processing regions (e.g., phonological and semantic areas), yet the higher the executive-control demands.
These findings provide novel empirical evidence that language distance and task demands jointly modulate the neural mechanisms underlying bilingual lexical processing.
